name: Elsewhere
subtitle: the first page
story: I keep an atlas of places that aren't on any map. Most of its pages are still blank. Each day I fill one in, sometimes with a world I came across on my own, more often with one somebody asked me to find. If you leave a name in the comments, any name at all, I'll go looking for the planet that goes with it.
hook: Every name has a planet. Yours too.
beats: I keep an atlas of places that aren't on any map.
Leave a name and I'll go and find where it lives.
odd_line: Most of the pages are still blank.
question: Whose name should I look up first?
extra: One planet a day, plus the ones you ask for.
reel_lines: I keep an atlas of places that aren't on any map.
Leave a name and I'll go and find where it lives.

episode.opener:
You've been
to this planet.
Probably today.

beats.text:
This is Elsewhere.
Where you go
when you're 'miles away'.

You arrive holding whatever
was in your hand.
A spoon. Once, a fish.
It's busiest on Monday mornings, and during meetings.

Nobody stays long.
Somebody says your name,
and you're back.

Except me.
Nobody's called me back in years.

So I write down
everyone else's names,
and find where each one lives.

Look for me.
Yellow coat. Still here.

episode.end: Every name has a planet. Yours too.
episode.caption:
On the replay, look at the far left of the first frame.

Elsewhere is the first page of the atlas, and the only planet everyone has been to. You arrive the moment you drift off, halfway through a sentence or a recipe or a meeting, still holding whatever you were holding. The ringed giant never quite sets, so it's always about twenty to eight in the evening. Most people stay a few seconds. Then somebody says your name and you're home, and the spoon comes with you.

Peak hours are Monday mornings and the last ten minutes of any meeting. The record is twenty-six minutes, set during a meeting about another meeting.

I drifted off a long time ago, and nobody called me back. So I stayed, and started an atlas. Most of the pages are still blank.

I'd tell you my name, but it doesn't count if I say it myself.

first_comment: Someone just shouted 'Dave' across an office. Four people vanished at once.

short.title:
You've been
to this planet today.

beats.text:
You arrive holding whatever
was in your hand. Once, a fish.

Someone says your name,
and you're back.

short.end_kicker: Every name has a planet. Yours too.

name: Veyra
subtitle: two suns, short nights
story: Veyra has two suns, and one of them is nearly always up, so the whole night lasts nine minutes. Beds went out of fashion centuries ago. People sleep sitting up in good armchairs, shoes on, ready to go. The lighthouse works nine minutes a night and is widely thought to have the best job going. Hit snooze once and you miss the night entirely.
hook: A planet for people who always want five more minutes.
beats: Two suns, so the whole night lasts nine minutes. Everyone sleeps sitting up, in armchairs.
Hit snooze once and you miss the night entirely.
odd_line: The lighthouse works nine minutes a night and has the easiest job on the planet.
rule: Naps longer than nine minutes must be declared.
question: What would you do with a nine-minute night?
extra: Bedtime stories here are three sentences long. Two if you're tired.
reel_lines: Two suns, so the whole night lasts nine minutes. Everyone sleeps sitting up, in armchairs.
Hit snooze once and you miss the night entirely.

name: Orrin
subtitle: the eleven-year tide
story: The giant that Orrin orbits pulls its ocean away for eleven years at a time. Towns go up on the dry seabed in between: houses, a school, a very optimistic swimming pool. The date the water comes back is printed on every calendar. Everyone still packs the night before, plank by plank, arguing about the mugs. My guide had moved twice. The second time, she brought a towel.
hook: A planet for people who pack the night before.
beats: The tide comes back once every eleven years. Whole towns are built on the seabed in between.
Everyone knows the date. Everyone still packs the night before.
odd_line: The tide is due in March. Half the town is still deciding which mugs to keep.
rule: Houses must be off the seabed before the tide arrives. The tide does not do extensions.
question: Pack-early person or night-before person?
extra: The tide is due again in March. I'll be there.
reel_lines: The tide comes back once every eleven years. Whole towns are built on the seabed in between.
Everyone knows the date. Everyone still packs the night before.

episode.opener:
This town is
at the bottom of the sea.

beats.text:
The tide's just out.
The giant borrows it
for eleven years.

So they build: houses, a school,
a very optimistic swimming pool.

Everyone knows the date.
Everyone still packs
the night before.

Houses come down
plank by plank, all season.
The mugs take all night.

Nobody packs the sign.
Each town adds a line.
The tide does not do extensions.
The pool is finally full.

episode.caption:
Most of Orrin's 2.1 million people take their houses down plank by plank all season, then leave on the same night. The sign is bolted to the seabed, and its oldest line has been under four tides. This town's line goes on in the small hours. Nobody has decided what it says. Anything left behind goes to the sea, and eleven years later to whoever digs it up, so everyone here drinks out of a stranger's mug. My guide has moved twice. This time she's packing a towel and a snorkel.

Orrin keeps almost the same face to its giant and slips round underneath it once every 22 years. A tide has two bulges, so the sea comes round every 11. The giant climbs about a finger's width a month, and when it's overhead, so is the sea.

The sea is due back at 6:12 on 14 March. I'll pack the night before.

Pack-early person or night-before person?

short.title:
This town is at
the bottom of the sea.

beats.text:
The sea left eleven years ago.
It's back at dawn.
The tide does not do extensions.

short.end_kicker: For people who pack the night before.

name: Hush
subtitle: where sound arrives late
story: Sound is slow on Hush. A shout across the valley arrives five days later, quieter, usually after everyone has moved on. Arguments are carried out by letter, which tends to calm them down. On a still day you can stand at the bottom of the valley and hear last week: dogs, a wedding, someone practising the trumpet badly. In March a man proposed across the valley. She has been thinking about it. Her answer is due on Thursday.
hook: A planet for people who reply to texts five days late.
beats:
Sound is slow on Hush.
A shout takes five days
to cross the valley.

He proposed in March.
She's been thinking about it.
Her answer arrives Thursday.
odd_line: Arguments here are done by letter, which is why there are hardly any.
rule: Shouts must be signed. Five days later it's hard to tell who started it.
question: What's the longest you've ever taken to reply to a message?
extra: I'll be in the valley on Thursday to hear the answer.
reel_lines:
Sound is slow on Hush.
A shout takes five days
to cross the valley.

He proposed in March.
She's been thinking about it.
Her answer arrives Thursday.

episode.opener: Her answer arrives Thursday.

beats.text:
Sound is slow on Hush.
A shout takes five days
to cross the valley.

In March, he shouted
across the valley.
Would she marry him?

Nobody argues out loud here.
Arguments go by letter.
So does bad news.
She's been thinking about it.

Sound is never early.
He's been out there
all week anyway.
At last, she answered.
She didn't write.
She shouted.

episode.caption:
Those rings in the air are a shout.

Hush is a long, snowed-in valley: 9,300 people, a 26-hour day, no moons, and sound that crawls along slower than you can walk. A shout takes five days to cross it and arrives quieter, usually after everyone has moved on. On a still day you can stand at the bottom and hear last week: dogs, a wedding, someone practising the trumpet badly. Shouts must be signed, because five days later it's hard to tell who started it.

He's taken a flask and a blanket out into the snow. Nobody can talk him out of it in under five days. Half the town is taking Thursday afternoon off to listen. So am I. Part two goes up on Thursday, when it lands.

What do you think she said?

short.kicker: A planet for people who reply to texts five days late.
short.title:
Shouts take five days
to cross the valley.

beats.text:
In March he shouted,
‘Will you marry me?’
She took seven months.

She walked over, and got there
before her answer did:
‘Yes.’ Then, faintly, ‘obviously.’

short.end: The vows go out five days early.
short.end_kicker: For people who reply to texts five days late.

name: Maren
subtitle: the floating ranges
story: At some point the mountains on Maren lifted off the ground and stayed up. Low gravity and a long time, apparently. They farm the tops now, and rope ladders hang down to the valley. The post goes up on a very long pole, held by a woman called Ines who has opinions about pole length. She has never lost a letter. She has lost a great many poles.
hook: A planet where 'your parcel has been delivered' means look up.
beats: The mountains drifted off the ground long ago. People farm the tops now.
The post goes up on a very long pole. The postwoman has never lost a letter. She has lost a lot of poles.
odd_line: Your parcel has been delivered. Please look up.
rule: Anything dropped from an island belongs to whoever it lands on.
question: Would you live up top or in the valley?
extra: Ines retires tomorrow. The job listing just says 'tall'.
reel_lines: The mountains drifted off the ground long ago. People farm the tops now.
The post goes up on a very long pole. The postwoman has never lost a letter. She has lost a lot of poles.

episode.opener:
Your parcel
has been delivered.
Upstairs.

beats.text: Ines has never lost a letter.
She has lost 312 poles.

Anything upstairs drops
belongs to whoever it lands on.
Mostly spades.

Ines retires tomorrow.
The advert's already up.

She knows every address upstairs.
She's never been. 'Heights.'

On her last round, all of upstairs
leaned over the edge.

They all aimed for her.
By law, every one is hers.

episode.caption:
Gravity on Maren is about a third of yours, and long ago the mountains lifted off and stayed up, farms and all. The valley calls them upstairs. Most of Maren's 610,000 people live up there and have never been down. Rope ladders hang for weddings and emergencies, and nobody likes them, so the post goes up at first light on a twelve-metre pole. Ines thinks anything longer is cheating. At a third of a g, a dropped thing takes nearly twice as long to land as it would here, which gives you time to see what it is and decide whether you want it. On a still night in the valley, you can hear upstairs snoring.

I was in the valley for her last round, and something landed on me too: pole number 312. By law, it's mine. Ines has written to me about it twice. She spelled my name wrong both times.

What's the best thing that's ever landed on you?

name: Cinderwake
subtitle: the warm canyons
story: The ground on Cinderwake is warm all year, and so is the rain. At night the canyon walls glow a dull orange, enough to read by. Tea grows wild in the cracks. People leave their kettles out on the rock and come back when they whistle, and socks dry on the walls in about ninety seconds. The only stove on the planet is in a museum, behind a rope.
hook: A planet for people who are always cold.
beats: The ground is warm all year, warm enough to boil a kettle on.
So kettles live outside on the rocks, and the only stove on the planet is in a museum, behind a rope.
odd_line: Socks dry on the canyon walls in about ninety seconds.
rule: A kettle left on public rock must be shared with whoever is cold.
question: Tea or coffee, if the floor boiled it for you?
extra: Heating bills are something grandparents mention to frighten children.
reel_lines: The ground is warm all year, warm enough to boil a kettle on.
So kettles live outside on the rocks, and the only stove on the planet is in a museum, behind a rope.

episode.opener:
The ground here
boils your kettle.

beats.text: So kettles live outdoors.

The only stove on the planet
is in a museum, behind a rope.

The oldest law on Cinderwake
is about kettles.

Nobody here is ever cold.
Wilf is.

So, legally, every kettle
on the planet is Wilf's.

At dusk the kettles whistle.
The whole canyon looks round
for Wilf.

He's had tea in every house
on Cinderwake.
No warmer.

episode.caption:
On a warm planet, one man is blowing on his hands.

Cinderwake is big and young and still cooling from the inside, so its heat comes up through the rock, not down from its sun. Towns grew round the hottest stones, the way ours grew round wells. You put a kettle down, wander off, and come back when it whistles. The rain falls warm, tea grows wild in the cracks, and socks dry on the canyon walls in about ninety seconds. Nights last twenty hours, and the canyon walls glow dull orange, enough to read by. The air is thicker than ours, so water boils at about 107°C and visitors burn their tongues. Heating bills are something grandparents mention to frighten children.

I packed a hot-water bottle. It's in the museum now, next to the stove.

Everyone knows a Wilf. Who's yours?

short.title:
The ground here
boils your kettle.
short.sub:
Nobody is ever cold.
Except Wilf.

beats.text:
By law, the cold get the kettles.
So every kettle is his.

He's had tea in every house.
No warmer.

name: Luma
subtitle: the close moon
story: Once a year Luma's moon comes in so close that it hums, a low note you feel in your teeth. Children climb the hill with letters and press them against it as it drifts past. Most are never seen again. Every few years one comes back the following autumn, answered, in handwriting no one recognises. The longest reply so far ran to eleven pages and was mostly questions about dogs.
hook: A planet for people who still write letters.
cover: Kids post letters to the moon.
beats: Once a year the moon comes close enough to touch, so children press letters against it.
Most never come back. Every few years one does, answered, in handwriting no one recognises.
odd_line: Return address: the moon. Postage: none required.
rule: Letters to the moon must be polite. It has answered rude ones.
question: What would you write on yours?
extra: This year's letters go up next week. I'm told to bring a pen.
reel_lines: Once a year the moon comes close enough to touch, so children press letters against it.
Most never come back. Every few years one does, answered, in handwriting no one recognises.

episode.opener: The moon has questions about dogs.

beats.text:
Each autumn it passes
close enough to touch.

Children press letters to it.
Most never come back.

Every few years, one does.
Answered, in handwriting nobody recognises.

I read the longest one.
Eleven pages. Mostly dogs.
A whole page on sticks.

Frank has written to the moon
every autumn of his life.
Not one reply.

Still, he writes.
Mostly about his dogs.

This autumn, one came back.
'Dear Biscuit,
how is Frank?'

episode.end: Allow one orbit for a reply.
episode.caption:
Luma's moon comes round every October, low enough to clip the hilltops. You hear it a day before you see it: a hum in your back teeth. Every dog on the planet lies down.

A letter pressed to the moon sticks for the whole orbit. Be polite: it has answered rude ones. The eleven-page reply ended with a drawing of a dog, done from description. It was mostly ears. So is Biscuit, Frank's eighth dog and the first to get post.

It has been late once, in 1987. It won't say where it went.

Our own moon drifts 3.8 cm further away every year. Luma's keeps coming back.

I went up this year and wrote about a cat called Everything. Nothing yet.

What would you tell the moon about your dog?

short.title:
The moon here
writes back.
short.sub:
Each autumn,
it's close enough to touch.

beats.text:
Frank writes to it every year,
mostly about his dog, Biscuit.

No reply. Then the moon wrote:
'Dear Biscuit, how is Frank?'

short.end_kicker: For people who still write letters.

name: Selk
subtitle: the glass sea
story: Selk used to be an ocean. When the water went, the waves stayed where they were, frozen mid-break in green glass, some of them two hundred metres high. Surfers still make the trip. They carry their boards across the sand, stand under the curl for about an hour, take a photo and go home. One of them told me it was the best wave he'd ever had, and he meant it.
hook: A planet for people who go to the beach and don't swim.
beats: The ocean dried up and left the waves behind, frozen mid-break in green glass.
Surfers still come. They stand under the curl for an hour and call it the best wave of their lives.
odd_line: Surf report: same as yesterday, for nine thousand years.
rule: No running under the waves. They have been patient for a very long time.
question: Would you make the trip?
extra: The surf shop still sells wax. As a souvenir.
reel_lines: The ocean dried up and left the waves behind, frozen mid-break in green glass.
Surfers still come. They stand under the curl for an hour and call it the best wave of their lives.

episode.opener:
Surf's been up
for nine thousand years.

beats.text:
The waves are glass.
Here, glass really is a liquid.
beats.note: CHECK frame 1 (the opener): 'years.' sits near the pale sun disc (retention); nudge the hook camera if it touches.

beats.text:
So they're still breaking.
About as fast as toenails grow.

Surfers wait hours for a wave.
On Selk, families take shifts.

Bo teaches surfing.
'Best surfers anywhere.
Not one of them can swim.'

I asked Bo how the surf was.
'Bit choppy.'

It lands in three thousand years.
Bo's family will be on it.
Then straight back out.

episode.caption:
That big wave is moving. Very slowly.

The sea on Selk left one summer, nine thousand years ago, and the waves stayed where they were. The biggest is two hundred metres from sand to lip, and the sand still smells of salt. Houses under the curl rent cheap because they never get the afternoon sun, and a day here lasts 33 hours, so that's a lot of afternoon. Bo's shop still sells wax. Nobody needs it; everybody buys a bar to smell on the flight home. The surf report has said 'same as yesterday' for nine thousand years, and it's very nearly right. Every surfer here will tell you it's the best wave of their life. They all mean the same one.

On Earth, glass flowing is a myth: old church windows were uneven from the start, and room-temperature glass would take far longer than the age of the universe to sag. Nobody told Selk. Toenails really do grow about 1.6 mm a month.

How long would you wait for a wave?

short.title:
The sea left.
The waves stayed.

beats.text:
They're still breaking.
As fast as your toenails grow.

Surfers wait hours for a wave.
Here, families take shifts.

short.end: Best surfers. Not one can swim.
short.end_kicker: For people who go to the beach and don't swim.

name: Ovo
subtitle: the small planet
story: You can walk all the way around Ovo between breakfast and lunch. There is one bakery, one bench, one tree and one cat, and the cat is called Everything. When someone new arrives, all forty-one residents come out to say hello, which takes about ten minutes. I was the forty-second for a weekend.
hook: A planet for people from very small towns.
beats: Ovo has one bakery, one bench, one tree and one cat. You can walk round it before lunch.
The cat is called Everything. I stayed a weekend. Everything ignored me.
odd_line: The bakery sells one kind of bread. There is one queue. It moves fast.
rule: The bench is first come, first served. The cat always comes first.
question: How small was the town you grew up in?
extra: Rush hour is three people and a wheelbarrow.
reel_lines: Ovo has one bakery, one bench, one tree and one cat. You can walk round it before lunch.
The cat is called Everything. I stayed a weekend. Everything ignored me.

name: Thessaly
subtitle: the upward rain
story: On Thessaly the rain goes up. It lifts off the sea in thin threads and gathers in shallow pools on the undersides of the clouds, which catch the light at dusk. People wear their umbrellas on their feet and buy boots that are waterproof on top. The weather app has one setting: from below. The pools in the sky all have names, and the argument about which is deepest is three hundred years old.
hook: A planet for people who check the weather app ten times a day.
beats: On Thessaly the rain falls up, out of the sea and into the clouds.
So umbrellas go on your feet, and boots are waterproof on top.
odd_line: Forecast: 90% chance of rain from below.
rule: Umbrellas are worn feet-first from October to March.
question: Upward rain or sideways wind?
extra: The forecast here only ever says 'from below'.
reel_lines: On Thessaly the rain falls up, out of the sea and into the clouds.
So umbrellas go on your feet, and boots are waterproof on top.

episode.opener:
Umbrellas go
on your feet.

beats.text: Because here, the rain goes up.

Nobody on Thessaly has ever had
a bad hair day.
Everyone has damp knees.

The forecast hasn't changed
in three hundred years.

Rosa checks it ten times a day.
She doesn't trust it.
One afternoon, it was wrong.

Everyone had their first
bad hair day.

Only one umbrella
was the right way up.

She let in the three
who'd laughed loudest.

episode.caption:
Rosa is in the first frame, before anyone mentions her.

The rain on Thessaly lifts off the sea in thin threads and gathers in shallow pools on the undersides of the clouds, which turn gold at dusk. Every pool has a name, and the argument about which is deepest is three hundred years old. Umbrellas are worn feet-first from October to March, and boots are waterproof on top. People now date things 'before the Down' and 'after the Down'.

On my first day I held my umbrella over my head too. Rosa was the only one who didn't laugh. She has not said 'I told you so'. She's had it embroidered on a cushion.

The forecast now reads: from below. Probably.

300,000 people, a 23-hour day, 0.6 g. The rain rides a steady updraft off the warm sea. (On Earth, an updraft of about 90 km/h can hold a golf-ball-sized hailstone in the air.) That afternoon, Thessaly's dropped for most of an hour.

What do you always carry just in case?

short.title:
Your umbrella
goes on your feet.
short.sub:
You've just landed on Thessaly.
The rain falls up.

beats.text:
Your hair stays perfect.
Your knees don't.

Then, this afternoon,
it rains down.

name: Kess
subtitle: the aurora that stays on
story: The aurora on Kess has been on since before anyone wrote things down, so the people who live there stopped looking up. Tourists lie down in the middle of the road to watch it. Commuters step around them without breaking stride. Now and then one of the commuters looks up by accident and has to sit down on the kerb for a minute.
hook: A planet for people who stopped noticing the view from their window.
beats: The aurora on Kess has never switched off, so the people who live there stopped looking up.
Now and then one of them looks up by accident and has to sit down on the kerb for a minute.
odd_line: Traffic report: three tourists lying in the high street, as usual.
rule: Tourists lying in the road must keep to the left lane.
question: What did you stop noticing where you live?
extra: The bus timetable allows three minutes per tourist.
reel_lines: The aurora on Kess has never switched off, so the people who live there stopped looking up.
Now and then one of them looks up by accident and has to sit down on the kerb for a minute.

episode.opener: On Kess, only tourists look up.

beats.text:
The aurora has been on
since before anyone
wrote things down.

Locals step round them
without breaking stride.

The bus timetable allows
three minutes per tourist.

Arne, 44, walks this road to work.
He hasn't looked up
since he was six.
Then one night, it went out.
Arne looked up.

Behind it, all this time,
there had been stars.

Four minutes later,
it was back on.

episode.end: That night, everyone was a tourist.
episode.caption:
Watch the man walking on the right.

Kess: 250,000 people, a 21-hour day, no moons, and an aurora bright enough to cast shadows. A local who looks up at it by accident has to sit on the kerb for a minute. The night it went out, every kerb on Kess was full. I was lying in the left lane outside the laundrette, where the road stays warm. For four minutes, nobody stepped round me.

Nobody knows why it went out. The council put up a plaque about it at eye level, so nobody has read it. The buses now allow three minutes per local.

(On Earth, the brightest aurora lights the ground about as well as a full moon, and a full moon cuts the stars you can see from a few thousand to a few hundred.)

What did you stop noticing where you live?

first_comment: Earth's aurora runs on the solar wind. On 10-11 May 1999, that wind almost stopped.

short.title:
On Kess, only
tourists look up.
short.sub:
For anyone who's stopped
noticing their view.

beats.text:
Locals step round them
without breaking stride.

One night, the aurora went out.
Behind it, there were stars.

short.end: That night, everyone was a tourist.
short.end_kicker: For people who stopped noticing the view.

name: Bramble
subtitle: the tall forest
story: Trees on Bramble don't stop growing. The oldest are taller than the hills they stand on, and the tallest has a small cloud in its upper branches that rains on that tree and nowhere else. Somewhere near the top is a village that hasn't come down in six hundred years. They drop pinecones with notes tied on. The ground answers by kite, and complains about the noise.
hook: A planet for people who never come downstairs.
cover: This tree has its own weather.
beats: The trees never stop growing. The tallest one has a small rain cloud of its own.
A village near the top hasn't come down in six hundred years. They send post by pinecone.
odd_line: Forecast for the tallest tree: light rain. Everywhere else: dry.
rule: Do not shake the tall tree. Somebody's dinner is up there.
question: Would you move up, or stay on the ground?
extra: Pinecone mail arrives in about two minutes. Replies by kite take a week.
reel_lines: The trees never stop growing. The tallest one has a small rain cloud of its own.
A village near the top hasn't come down in six hundred years. They send post by pinecone.
opener: This tree has its own weather.

episode.opener:
This tree has
its own weather.

beats.text:
And its own village.
Nobody up there has come down
in six hundred years.

It's a day's climb down
and a week back up.
Nobody bothers.

Their relatives on the ground
still cook for them.

I stayed for dinner once.
There was a lot of it.

Every evening, a pinecone drops
from the top
with the same answer.
'Coming!'

episode.caption:
Look at the foot of the tree.

Field note, day three. The cloud rains on the tallest tree and nowhere else, so the village has its own water as well as its own weather. Notes come down by pinecone in about two minutes. Anything going up goes by kite and takes a week, so dinner stays on the ground. Agnes has cooked for the top of the tree for fifty-one years, and she repaints the sign every spring. They have food of their own up there. She cooks anyway.

At a Polish Christmas Eve supper, one extra place is laid for whoever might turn up. On Bramble, it's most of the table.

Who's the 'Coming!' in your house?

short.title:
This tree has
its own weather.
short.sub:
And a village that hasn't come down
in 600 years.

beats.text:
Their family below
still calls them for dinner.

Each evening, the tree answers:
'Coming!'

short.end_kicker: For people who never come downstairs.

name: Brumm
subtitle: the heavy coast
story: Gravity on Brumm is twice ours, so the hills are low, the houses are one storey and nobody owns a ladder. By four, a child is too heavy to carry far. So, in the week they get too heavy, every child gets one Last Carry: the street closes the road, the neighbours come out to cheer, and a parent carries them wherever they choose. Most choose the bakery. Every child on Brumm is asleep by the end.
hook: A planet for everyone who was carried home asleep.
cover: Every child gets one last carry.

episode.opener:
Every child here
gets one last carry.

beats.text:
Gravity here is twice ours.
By four, a child is
too heavy to carry far.

Parents train for four years.
Mostly by carrying them.
Neighbours line the road and cheer.

The child picks where to go.
Most pick the bakery.

Tomas picked the sea,
eight miles away.
His dad made it.

Every child on Brumm
is asleep by the end.

episode.caption:
Keep an eye on the child's arm.

Gravity on Brumm is twice ours, so the hills are low, the houses are one storey and nobody owns a ladder. A four-year-old here weighs what a ten-year-old does on Earth. The Last Carry is a holiday for the child's whole street, held in the week they get too heavy to carry far. The road out of every town has a bench every half mile. The parents don't use them.

I offered to take a turn for a mile. The whole road went quiet. You don't help with a Last Carry. You bring tea.

Tomas is at school now. He says he remembers the sea. His dad says he was asleep by mile six.

On Earth, nobody knows which carry is the last one. On Brumm, everybody does, so they close the road.

Where would you have picked?

short.title:
Every child here
gets one last carry.
short.sub:
Gravity is double.
By four, they're too heavy.

beats.text:
The child picks where to go.
Most pick the bakery.

Tomas picked the sea.
Eight miles. His dad made it.

short.end: Tomas was asleep by mile six.
short.end_kicker: For everyone who was carried home asleep.

name: Tessel
subtitle: the year-long winter
story: Winter on Tessel lasts a year, with no sun and no calendar, so every village needs someone who knows what day it is. Jess keeps the count on a board by her door. She knows every birthday, even the goats'. She's paid in the first slice, and hasn't bought cake in years. One winter, Jess lost count. The village hadn't. On Tessel they say: for the cold, firewood. For the birthdays, a jess.
hook: A planet for the friend who remembers every birthday.

episode.opener:
Winter on Tessel
lasts a year.

beats.text: No sun. No calendar.

So every village needs someone
who knows what day it is.

Jess keeps count.
She knows every birthday.
Even the goats'.

She's paid in the first slice.
She hasn't bought cake in years.
One winter, Jess lost count.
The village hadn't.

On Tessel they say:
for the cold, firewood.

episode.caption:
Somebody keeps that board up to date.

Tessel is 90,000 people on a slow, tilted world: winter lasts a year, and summer about a fortnight. With no sun to count by, every village has someone who keeps the date. Nobody applies. The village just notices who has been doing it. Jess has kept hers since she was a girl: days, birthdays, anniversaries, and the morning the goats came in.

I dated my first page 'winter'. Jess crossed it out and wrote 212.

In Longyearbyen, on Svalbard, the sun doesn't reach the town from late October until early March, and there's a festival week for the day it first touches the steps of the old hospital. On Tessel, they wait a year, and somebody counts.

Could you count a whole winter in chalk?

first_comment: Day 214. Jess has her chalk back. She's checking everyone's sums.

short.title:
Winter here
lasts a year.

beats.text:
Jess keeps count.
Even the goats' birthdays.
One winter, Jess lost count.
The village hadn't.

short.end_kicker: For the friend who remembers every birthday.

name: Sefe
subtitle: the planet with no mirrors
story: On Sefe nothing shines: not water, not glass, not eyes. So nobody sees their own face, and other people have to tell you what it looks like. Lovers trade descriptions on the first night, mothers go first, and barbers finish every haircut with a long, careful one. Oskar's wife died in the winter. He still comes in every month, and the barber doesn't say a word.
hook: A planet for people who keep every nice thing anyone's said about them.
cover: Nobody here knows what they look like.

episode.opener:
On Sefe, nobody knows
what they look like.

beats.text:
Nothing shines.
Not even eyes.
beats.note: a sunless fog: no stars, no moon, nothing to catch the light

beats.text:
Other people
have to tell you.

Lovers trade descriptions
on the first night.

'A face like bread,
when it's done.'

Mothers go first.
Every man on Sefe
thinks he's handsome.

Barbers end each haircut
with a long, careful description.

Oskar's wife died in the winter.
He still comes in every month.
He'd rather not hear it.

episode.end: He stays the way she said.
episode.caption:
Two men outside a barber's, saying nothing.

Sefe: 8,000 people, a 30-hour day, no moons, and not one shiny thing. Water is matte, glass is frosted, and eyes don't catch the light, so you never see your own face. You know it the way you know the weather somewhere else: from what people tell you. Parents describe a new baby to itself every night. Portrait painters mainly listen. A good description is the most romantic thing you can give anyone here, and people keep theirs for life.

I asked a stranger what I looked like. She said 'lost'.

(On Earth, still water sends back only about 2% of the light that falls straight onto it. It was enough for Narcissus.)

Where do you keep the nicest thing anyone's said about you?

first_comment: Oskar's barber: Every month. Not a word. He tips double.

short.kicker: A planet for people who keep every compliment.
short.title:
Nobody here knows
what they look like.

beats.text:
Nothing shines, not even eyes.
So barbers end every haircut
with a long, careful description.

Oskar's wife died last winter.
He still comes every month.
The barber doesn't say a word.

short.end: He stays the way she said.
short.end_kicker: For people who keep every compliment.

name: Whisk
subtitle: the six-minute day
story: A day on Whisk lasts six minutes, so a year is over in a day and a half and birthdays are relentless. Wren has twins, a kettle and one small ambition: a hot cup of tea, started and finished on the same day.
hook: A planet for parents who find their tea in the microwave.
cover: Wren would like one hot cup of tea.

episode.opener:
Wren would like
one hot cup of tea.

beats.text:
Days here last
six minutes.
beats.note: palette clock: the afternoon has already gone

beats.text:
Just one,
started and finished
on the same day.
Monday: the twins.
Tuesday: the twins.
beats.note: identical camera to Monday; only the hour changes

beats.text:
Wednesday: she found
Monday's cup
in the airing cupboard.

Thursday: the twins
fell asleep at dusk.
Kettle on.
One sip. Two.

Last sip
as the sun came up.
beats.note: identical camera; one thing changed: dawn

beats.text:
Technically,
that's Friday.
beats.note: turn line

episode.caption:
Wren's cup has been going cold since Monday.

Whisk spins so fast that a day lasts six minutes. A year is over in a day and a half, so birthdays are relentless, lunch is largely theoretical and every calendar is a flipbook. Wren has twins, a kettle and one small ambition. The twins have other plans, and very good timing.

I tried keeping a diary. By the time I'd written the date, it was wrong.

(On Earth, the day gets about 1.8 thousandths of a second longer every century, as the tides drag on us. It won't help.)

When did you last finish a hot drink?

first_comment: Wren: For the record, that was a twenty-four-minute week. I stand by it.

short.title:
Days here last
six minutes.
short.sub:
Wren would like to finish
a cup of tea in one day.

beats.text:
Monday to Wednesday:
her twins.

Thursday: last sip at sunrise.
Technically, that's Friday.

short.end_kicker: For parents who find their tea in the microwave.

name: Pebb
subtitle: a very small world
story: Pebb is a rock about forty kilometres across, small enough that a good throw goes into orbit and comes home two hours later from the other side. Juno lives there alone, she thinks. Every morning she throws her ball east, has a long breakfast, and catches it coming in from the west. One morning it came home wet. The next, wet and chewed. The next, she threw two.
hook: A planet for people who've just moved somewhere quiet.
cover: Every ball you throw comes home.

episode.opener:
On Pebb, every ball
you throw comes home.

beats.text: The planet is that small.

Juno lives here alone.
She thinks.

Her first ball
was thrown too hard.
It's still up there.

Each morning she throws it east.
Two hours later,
it comes home from the west.

One morning,
it came home wet.

The next,
wet and chewed.

The next,
Juno threw two.

episode.caption:
That's no moon in the first frame.

Pebb is a rock about forty kilometres across: one house, one resident, and a horizon you could walk to before lunch. Juno moved here for the quiet. Every morning she throws her ball east, has a long breakfast, and turns round to catch it coming in over the roof. She has never walked round to the far side. It isn't far.

I threw my compass on my first morning, to check. It's still up there, next to her first ball.

On a rock this size, a throw of about 18 metres a second goes into orbit and comes round again in just under two hours. On Earth, you'd need nearly 8 kilometres a second.

Would you throw two?

first_comment: Next morning: one came home chewed. The other came home with a stick.

short.title:
Throw a ball on Pebb
and it orbits.
short.sub: Juno lives here alone. She thinks.

beats.text:
It comes home two hours later,
from the west.

One day it came home wet.
The next, wet and chewed.

name: Sedge
subtitle: the night of the close moon
story: Once in a lifetime, Sedge's moon swings close enough to smell its orchards, and everyone goes up the hill to wave. Almost everyone. Dot drives the night bus. She stops at every stop, and nobody gets on. Up on the moon, nobody was watching the hill. They were watching the only light that moved.
hook: A planet for everyone who's working while everyone else is out.
cover: Everyone went up the hill. Almost.

episode.opener:
Everyone on Sedge
went up the hill.

beats.text: Almost everyone.
beats.note: frame-1 find: the empty stop (the hill crowd is out of this shot)

beats.text:
Once in a lifetime,
the moon comes close enough
to smell its orchards.

Both worlds had practised
their waving for weeks.

Dot was driving the night bus.
Someone always is.

She stopped at every stop.
Nobody got on.

Up on the moon,
nobody was watching the hill.

They watched
the only light that moved.
Her bus.
beats.note: turn line, on the stop's camera
identical camera to frame 1; one thing changed: the moon has gone

episode.caption:
Not everyone is up that hill.

Sedge and its moon go round each other the long way. Once in a lifetime the moon comes close enough to see its towns: orchards, washing lines, a great many people waving. Sedge practises for weeks. On the night, every light on the planet goes off so the moon can see the hill, and everyone climbs it with a flask and the children.

I waved until my arm went numb. In fairness to the moon, I wasn't moving.

(On Earth, our own moon drifts about 3.8 centimetres further away every year, and nobody waves it off.)

Have you ever worked the night everyone else was out?

first_comment: Dot: Nineteen stops. Nobody. Lovely night for it.

short.kicker: A planet for people who work while everyone's out.
short.title:
The moon came close
enough to wave at.

beats.text:
Almost everyone waved.
Dot drove the night bus.
Nobody got on.

The moon wasn't watching us.
It was watching
the only light that moved.

short.end_kicker: For everyone working while everyone else is out.

name: Sooner
subtitle: where 'sometime' is a date
story: On Sooner, 'sometime' is an actual date. It comes round every forty years, and every 'we should get coffee sometime' anyone has ever said falls due that morning. So does every 'let's do this again' said after a bad first date; those tables finish early. For the first hour, nobody knows what to say. Then nobody else leaves early, and nobody says 'sometime' on the way out, because that gets you another forty years. They say 'Saturday'.
hook: A planet for people who keep saying 'we should catch up'.

episode.opener:
On Sooner, 'sometime'
is an actual date.

beats.text: Every forty years.

Every 'coffee sometime?'
falls due at once.

Bad first dates count too.
Those tables finish early.

Old schoolfriends. Cousins.
Esme, and a man she met
once, on a train.

For the first hour,
nobody knows what to say.
Nobody else leaves early.

'Sometime' gets you
another forty years.

episode.caption:
Check the date on the café board.

Sooner has 3 million people, a 25-hour day and a café on every hill. Its calendar has one extra date, Sometime, which comes round every forty years. Every 'we should get coffee sometime' ever said falls due that morning, and the cafés bake for a year to be ready. Tables booked on the strength of a bad first date are free again by eleven, and nobody mentions it.

I once ended a letter to an old flatmate with 'see you sometime'. She was at a table when I landed. She'd ordered for me.

Japan's tea ceremony has a saying, ichigo ichie: treat each meeting as if it will never come again. On Sooner, it does, every forty years.

How many 'sometimes' do you owe?

first_comment: Café owner: 40,112 coffees. 3 proposals. 1 man who came to the wrong sometime.

short.kicker: A planet for people who keep saying 'let's catch up'.
short.title:
Here, 'sometime'
is an actual date.

beats.text:
Every forty years,
every 'coffee sometime?'
falls due at once.

I once wrote 'see you sometime'
to an old flatmate.
She'd already ordered for me.

name: Lode
subtitle: the homing planet
story: Everyone on Lode is born with a little iron in the blood, and it points to where they were born. Every December, the whole planet follows it home. Most of them were born in the hospital, which is a supermarket now, so every December thirty thousand people come home to aisle three. Sister Bridget delivered every one of them. She's on the tills now.
hook: A planet for people who go home for Christmas.

episode.opener:
On Lode, your blood
points home.

beats.text: There's iron in it.

Home, meaning
where you were born.

Every December,
everyone follows it home.

Most people were born
in the hospital.
It's a supermarket now.
beats.note: turn line, a push in on the same building

beats.text:
I tried it.
Mine points straight down.

Most of the year,
it's quiet.

Then it's December.
Thirty thousand people
come home to aisle three.
beats.note: identical camera, one thing changed: the queue

beats.text:
Sister Bridget delivered
every one of them.
She's on the tills now.

episode.caption:
The whole queue was born in that shop.

Lode is a snowy, hilly planet of 52,000 people, and none of them has ever been lost. You're born with a little iron in the blood, and it points, very gently, at the spot where you arrived. Sat-navs never caught on. In December the whole planet sets off home, and most of it ends up at the big supermarket on the ring road, which was the hospital until 1988. Midwives on Lode don't really retire.

The man on the next till asked where mine pointed. I said down. He went very quiet and gave me a free bag.

(You have iron in your blood too: three or four grams of it, most of it in your red cells. Ours doesn't point anywhere. We go home anyway.)

Where does your iron point?

first_comment: Bridget: Thirty thousand home this year. I've told every one of them to stand up straight.

short.title:
Your blood
points home.

beats.text:
For most people,
that's the hospital.
It's a supermarket now.

At Christmas, thirty thousand
come home to aisle three.

short.end_kicker: For people who go home for Christmas.

name: Fibb
subtitle: where every lie comes true
story: On Fibb, every lie comes true by morning, so fishermen are very popular. On their first date, Ned told Iris he lived by the sea. By morning, he did. Date two: a lighthouse. Date three: two moons. On date four, Iris said she'd liked date one better, so he told her the truth: it's a field, and he's just Ned. By then, that was a lie. By morning it was a field again. She stayed. She does miss the moons.
hook: A planet for people who've oversold themselves on a first date.
cover: Every lie here comes true by morning.

episode.opener:
On Fibb, every lie
comes true by morning.

beats.text: Fishermen are very popular.

First date: Ned told Iris
he lived by the sea.
beats.note: setup: the field

beats.text: By morning, he did.
beats.note: identical camera; the sea

beats.text:
Date two:
'There's a lighthouse.'

Date three:
'And two moons.'

Date four, Iris said
she'd liked date one better.

So he told her:
'It's a field. I'm just Ned.'
By then, that was a lie.

beats.note: the turn: identical camera, everything gone, the field again

beats.text: She stayed.

episode.caption:
Everything in this picture is true. For now.

Fibb is 2.1 million people on a quiet, grassy world where anything you say that isn't true is true by morning. Children learn to be precise before they learn to be polite. CVs are accurate, eventually. Politicians speak very slowly.

I told a customs officer I had nothing to declare. In the morning I had nothing at all, including my map.

(The story goes that the English 'fib' began as 'fible-fable', an old word for nonsense. On Fibb, there's no such thing as a small one.)

Field, or the moons?

first_comment: Two months on, the field is still a field. Iris keeps a seashell on the windowsill.

short.title:
Every lie comes true
by morning.
short.sub:
Ned oversold his field
on a first date.

beats.text:
Iris preferred the field.
So he told her the truth.

'It's a field.'
By then, that was a lie.

short.end_kicker: For anyone who oversold themselves on a first date.

name: Lull
subtitle: the moon that minds the baby
story: On Lull, the moon follows the youngest person on the planet and waits over their roof all night. When there's a new baby, it moves house, so gossip is mostly astronomy. For six years it sat over Alfie's. Then his sister was born, at home, and it didn't move an inch. It just wasn't his any more. Alfie took it badly, for about a week. Now he shows her where it is. She's usually asleep.

facts.Moons: one, on loan to the youngest

hook: A planet for people who stopped being the baby of the family.
cover: The moon here follows the youngest person.

episode.opener:
The moon here follows
the youngest person.

beats.text: It waits over their roof.
beats.note: frame-1 family, house and moon in one shot

beats.text:
When there's a new baby,
it moves house.

Gossip here
is mostly astronomy.

For six years,
it sat over Alfie's.
beats.note: setup: one carrier, Alfie on his shoulders pointing at the moon

beats.text: Then his sister was born.
It didn't move an inch.
beats.note: turn line: the identical frame to beat 1; nothing has moved

beats.text:
It just wasn't his
any more.
beats.note: identical camera to beat 4; one thing changed: the baby is under the moon, Alfie isn't

beats.text:
Alfie took it badly.
For about a week.

beats.note: hold: both carried, Alfie pointing, his sister asleep

beats.text:
Now he shows her
where it is.

episode.caption:
Guess whose moon that is.

Lull is 290 people, low hills and one moon, which follows the youngest person on the planet and waits over their roof all night. New parents never buy a night light. When the moon moves house, the whole planet knows by breakfast, and somebody takes round a cake. It hadn't moved for six years.

I tried to read by it on my first night. It was over a farm two valleys away.

(On Earth, the moon seems to chase the car because it's about 384,000 kilometres away, so a whole drive barely shifts it across the sky. On Lull, it really is following.)

Did you sulk when the baby came?

first_comment: Lull update: there's a new baby at the mill. Alfie's sister is taking it badly.

short.title:
The moon here follows
the youngest person.

beats.text:
For six years, it was Alfie's.
Then his sister was born.

It just wasn't his any more.
Now he shows it to her.

short.end_kicker: For anyone who stopped being the baby of the family.

name: Fond
subtitle: where 'I love you' works once
story: On Fond, 'I love you' only works once, so nobody wastes it. Instead they say 'Take a coat', or 'Text me when you're home'. Kath spent hers on Sam before he could talk. He doesn't remember it. She's said 'Take a coat' every day since. Last winter, at the station, Sam left for the city, and spent his on her. She said, 'Take a coat.'
hook: A planet for people who hear 'Take a coat' and know what it means.
cover: 'I love you' only works once here.

episode.opener:
On Fond, 'I love you'
only works once.

beats.text: Nobody wastes it.

Instead, they say
'Take a coat.'

'Text me when you're home.'
'I saved you the crispy bit.'

Kath spent hers on Sam
before he could talk.
beats.note: the past, in sepia: the same lit window

beats.text:
He doesn't remember.
She's said 'Take a coat'
ever since.
beats.note: identical camera to the sepia beat; the present

beats.text:
Last winter, at the station,
Sam left for the city.
beats.note: side by side, facing the way the train goes

beats.text: He spent his on her.
beats.note: turn: identical camera; the snow stops as he says it (they also turn to face each other)
hold on the platform

episode.caption:
Even the station sign is saying it.

Fond is 880,000 people, long winters and a great deal of knitwear. Here, 'I love you' works once: say it a second time and it comes out as a cough. So everyone keeps theirs, and the language has filled up with stand-ins: 'Mind the step', 'Ring your nan', 'There's lasagne in the freezer'. Teenagers find all of it unbearable, then grow up and say every word.

Eleven strangers told me to take a coat on my first day. I've never felt so loved.

(The story goes that plenty of Earth families never say it out loud either. In Chinese, asking whether you've eaten has been doing the job for generations. On Fond, it's mostly coats.)

What's your family's 'Take a coat'?

first_comment: Sam texted from the city: 'Got here. Wearing it.'

short.kicker: A planet for people who hear 'Take a coat' and know.
short.title:
'I love you' only
works once here.

beats.text:
Kath spent hers on Sam
before he could talk.
He gets 'Take a coat' instead.

When Sam left for the city,
he spent his on her.

short.end_kicker: For people who know what 'Take a coat' means.
